query: For high-entropy-alloy materials intended for self-lubricating moving components, what single intervention could reduce both coefficient of friction and wear rate across a wide service-temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites prior evidence supporting it, and proposes an experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Integrating a controlled volume fraction of tungsten carbide (WC) into a high‐entropy alloy via a laser cladding surface modification process produces a composite surface that, through in situ formation of a self‐grinding edge and adaptive nanohierarchical tribolayer, significantly reduces both the coefficient of friction and wear rate across a wide service-temperature range compared to the untreated alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase or dual-phase high-entropy alloy (e.g., an AlCoCrFeNi-type system) without additional solid lubricants, exhibiting moderate friction and wear properties under sliding conditions.
generation.intervention: Laser cladding of the high-entropy alloy surface with a reinforcement of tungsten carbide (WC) particles in a controlled amount (e.g., 10-30 wt.%), forming an integrated composite coating.
generation.conditions: Under conditions typical for moving components – contact pressures up to about 0.9–1.0 GPa and service temperatures from room temperature to several hundred °C (e.g., up to 800 °C), where both abrasive and adhesive wear are active.
generation.structural_mediator: The intervention yields a composite microstructure with refined grains and dispersed WC-derived carbide phases that promote the formation of a self-adaptive, nanocrystalline, lubricious surface layer (or edge) during wear.
generation.mechanism: During sliding, the presence of WC particles leads to a self-grinding process that continuously regenerates the surface, while the refined microstructure and nanohierarchical tribolayer distribute contact stresses and reduce localized adhesion. This combination minimizes friction and wear via a synergistic mechanism of precipitation strengthening, adaptive surface reorganization, and inherent lubrication.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated alloy, the intervention is predicted to lower the average coefficient of friction (e.g., by 20–50%) and reduce wear rates by an order-of-magnitude or more, with these improvements maintained across the target temperature range.
generation.baseline: Untreated high-entropy alloy surfaces typically exhibit friction coefficients around 0.3–0.5 and wear rates on the order of 10^(-5) mm^3/(N·m) in comparable test conditions.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are anticipated only if the WC content and cladding parameters are optimized; excessive WC or non-uniform coatings could degrade ductility or lead to interface defects. Additionally, performance under extreme temperatures beyond the intended range or under different lubrication environments may not follow the predicted trend.
generation.uncertainty: While multiple studies suggest that nano-architectured surfaces and WC reinforcement can improve wear and friction performance, the exact magnitude of coefficient of friction reduction and wear rate improvement may vary with alloy composition, WC particle dispersion, and specific testing conditions, requiring further quantification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of test samples: one set of the base high-entropy alloy and one set modified by laser cladding with an optimized WC particle reinforcement. Subject both sets to identical ball-on-disk sliding wear tests under a range of temperatures (e.g., room temperature to 800 °C) and contact pressures. Ensure that coating uniformity and microstructural characteristics are characterized prior to testing.
measurements: Coefficient of friction (COF) measurements during sliding tests across the temperature range
Wear loss quantification (e.g., wear volume via profilometry) for both treated and untreated samples
Microstructural analysis of the worn surfaces (to verify formation of adaptive tribolayers)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the WC-modified high-entropy alloy coating does not show a statistically significant reduction (e.g., >20% lower COF and at least one order-of-magnitude lower wear rate) compared to the untreated alloy across the full test temperature range, or if the expected self-lubricating tribolayer is absent during post-test analysis.

Remarkable Wear Resistance in a Complex Concentrated Alloy with Nanohierarchical Architecture and Composition Undulation

Abstract: AbstractSustained wear damages on the sliding surfaces of alloys are generally the culprit responsible for the failure of various mechanical systems. Inspired by high-entropy effects, here we deliberately deploy nanohierarchical architecture with composition undulation in a Ni50(AlNbTiV)50 complex concentrated alloy, which yields ultralow wear rate within the order of 10−7 to 10−6 mm3/Nm between room temperature and 800 °C. Such remarkable wear resistance heretofore represents one of the highest wear resistance reported for the bulk alloys or composites, and originates from the multi-type adaptive friction interface protection governed by intrinsically nano-coupled grains and nanoprecipitates. This cooperative heterostructure releases gradient frictional stress in stages upon wear at room temperature through the coexistence of multiple deformation pathways while activating a dense nanocrystalline glaze layer upon wear at 800 °C to minimize adhesive and oxidative wear. Study on Microstructure and Properties of WC Particle-Reinforced FeCoCrNi-Matrix High Entropy Alloy Composites

Abstract: AbstractIn recent years, high entropy alloy (HEA) matrix composites have undergone rapid development. In this work, the effects of different WC contents (10 wt.%, 20 wt.%, and 30 wt.%) on the microstructure, mechanical properties, and wear resistance of FeCoCrNi HEA matrix composites prepared by spark plasma sintering (SPS) were studied. The results show that the WC–HEA composites are mainly composed of an FCC matrix phase (Ni, Fe) and carbide phases (Cr7C3, Co3W3C, WC, etc.). The hardness of the 30 WC–HEA composites was the highest at 459.2 HV, which is 71.2% higher than the 268.3 HV of the pure matrix material. Similarly, the compressive yield strength of the 30 WC–HEA composite was the largest, reaching 1315.1 MPa, which is 112.1% higher than that of the pure matrix material. However, the compression deformation rate of the 30 WC–HEA composite significantly decreased to 16.6%. WC-High Entropy Alloy Reinforced Long Life Self-Grinding Silage Knife Prepared by Laser Cladding

Abstract: AbstractThe working environment of agricultural knives is bad, which makes the knives wear out easily. A wear resistant layer of AlCoCrFeNi high entropy alloy (HEA) reinforced by tungsten carbide (WC) was prepared by laser cladding on one side of the cutting edge of a 65 Mn silage knife. Both the effects of WC addition on the microstructure and mechanical properties of AlCoCrFeNi (WC)x (x = 0, 0.1, 0.2 and 0.3 in mass percentage) alloys were investigated. All experimental alloys displayed a crystalline structure of simple body centered cubic (BCC). The hardness of the cladding layer increases with the increase of WC content, and the hardness value enhances from 740 HV0.2 to 1060 HV0.2. A self-grinding edge was formed during working for the cladded knives. The cutting quality can be improved and the service life of agricultural knives can be increased meanwhile. The weight loss rate of untreated knives was about 2.64 times that of the cladded knives after a 76 h field experiment.Keywords: high entropy alloy, WC particles, self-grinding, microstructure, wear resistance
